prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "KE Holdings Inc." (ticker BEKE), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BEKE", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: KE Holdings Inc.
result.industry: Online and offline residential real estate brokerage and housing services platform (China)
markets: New home sales agency for developers in China
Home rental and property management (Carefree Rent)
Housing-related financial and other emerging services

mission.source: KE Holdings press release on its 2024 ESG report (April 17, 2025), which says the report is underpinned by its mission of 'admirable service, joyful living'
mission.plain: Make the people who help families find homes respected professionals, so that families live better.

about.plain: KE Holdings runs Beike, a big app and website in China where people look for homes to buy or rent, and Lianjia, a famous chain of real estate agent shops. When a family buys, sells or rents a home through one of its agents, or through the many partner agencies on its platform, KE earns a fee. It also fixes up and furnishes homes and manages apartments that owners rent out through it. It started as Lianjia in Beijing in 2001.
about.customers: Families buying, selling or renting homes in China, plus property developers who pay it to sell their new apartments.
about.everyday: It is like Zillow plus a nationwide chain of estate agents and a home-renovation company rolled into one, for Chinese cities.

money.plain: commissions and platform fees on second-hand home deals
renting out and managing owners' apartments
home loans help and other new services

result.summary: KE has a real but bounded advantage: its Agent Cooperation Network, building database and the Lianjia brand give it the largest housing-transaction network in China (RMB3.18 trillion GTV in 2025, about 60,000 stores and 540,000 agents at mid-2026), and network effects among agents, stores and buyers are hard for rivals to copy. But brokerage is a low-margin, cyclical, regulated business, China's housing market has been shrinking (new-home sales value fell 12.6% in 2025), and commission rates face policy pressure, so the moat protects share more than profits.

pricingPower.evidence: Commission rates are under policy and competitive pressure (the 2023 MOHURD/SAMR guidance on brokerage services urged lower fees), and in 2025 revenue grew only 1.2% while GTV fell 5.0% and gross margin dropped from 24.6% to 21.4%; margins recovered in Q2 2026 (gross margin 28.6%) through cost cuts and mix rather than price rises, while revenue fell 5.7%.

moats.evidence: Lianjia, founded in 2001, is one of China's best-known brokerage brands and Beike is a leading home-search app (45.7 million average mobile MAU in Q2 2026), but brokerage brands command little price premium.
Home buyers transact rarely and can use any agency; partner brokerage brands (Deyou and others) are bound by platform tools and fee splits, but could leave at moderate cost.

The Agent Cooperation Network lets agents from different brands share listings and split commissions, so more stores (60,274 at June 30, 2026) bring more listings, which attract more buyers and agents.
With RMB3,183.3 billion of GTV in 2025 it spreads technology, data and training costs over far more transactions than any rival, though agent commissions, the main cost, scale with volume.
Local brokerage markets support many agencies and low entry barriers; KE's new-home GTV of RMB890.9 billion was only about 11% of China's RMB8.39 trillion of new-home sales in 2025.
Its platform model (true-listing pledge, cross-brand commission sharing) was hard for traditional single-brand agencies like Centaline to copy without changing how they pay their own agents.
Its building dictionary database of property-level data and its standardised transaction, training and agent-rating systems took nearly two decades to build at Lianjia.
It has no exclusive licence or asset; agents and listings can move to other agencies.

customers.evidence: Beike is widely used (45.7 million average MAU in Q2 2026, down from 48.7 million a year earlier) and Lianjia's true-listing and service guarantees are well regarded, but home buying is infrequent, so repeat purchase and loyalty are inherently low; no NPS is published.

talent.evidence: Lianjia is known for training and higher-quality agents, but brokerage turnover is high and active agents fell 7.5% year on year to 454,571 at June 30, 2026; we found no major employer-ranking recognition.

product.evidence: Beike is China's largest housing transaction and service platform by GTV, with VR viewings and a large property database, but no independent benchmark shows it clearly best in class, and portals like Anjuke and Douyin compete for buyer attention.

competitors.name: 5i5j Holding Group (I Love My Home)
competitors.note: Large brokerage and rental-management chain in Beijing, Shanghai and other big cities.

competitors.name: Centaline Property
competitors.note: Traditional brokerage chain in Hong Kong and mainland cities competing for resale and new-home deals.

competitors.name: 58.com / Anjuke
competitors.note: Leading property listing portals that sell leads to agents, competing with Beike for buyers and agents.

competitors.name: Ziroom
competitors.note: Large long-term rental apartment operator competing with Beike's Carefree Rent.

competitors.name: Douyin (ByteDance)
competitors.note: Short-video and live-stream property marketing and lead generation for developers and agents.

competitors.name: Fangdd Network Group
competitors.note: Smaller online platform for new-home transactions via independent agents.

competitors.name: Tubatu (To8to)
competitors.note: Online home-renovation marketplace competing with Beike's renovation business.

competitors.name: Red Star Macalline
competitors.note: Home furnishing malls competing for furnishing spending.

competitors.name: Easyhome New Retail
competitors.note: Home furnishing and renovation retail chain.

competitors.name: Alibaba Group (Xianyu, Taobao auctions)
competitors.note: Online property auctions and peer-to-peer listings.

competitors.name: China Vanke
competitors.note: Developer with in-house sales teams and rental apartments (Port Apartment).

competitors.name: Longfor Group
competitors.note: Developer operating Guanyu rental apartments and in-house sales.

marketShare.market: China new-home sales (KE new-home GTV as a share of NBS new commercial housing sales value)

threats: A prolonged Chinese housing downturn: GTV fell 15.6% year on year in Q1 2026 and new-home sales value fell 12.6% nationally in 2025.
Regulatory caps or guidance pushing brokerage commission rates lower, and tighter rules on rental and platform businesses.
Developers' financial distress causing slow payment or bad debts on new-home commissions.
Content and lead-generation platforms such as Douyin and Anjuke, and AI search, pulling buyer traffic away from Beike.
Partner brands or top agents leaving the Agent Cooperation Network for rival platforms.
Low-margin, capital-intensive rental (Carefree Rent) and renovation businesses diluting returns.
US-China tensions and US delisting risk for Chinese ADRs; governance concerns over founders' share-based pay.

ceo.name: Stanley Yongdong Peng
ceo.background: Co-founder; electrical engineering and automation degree from Zhejiang University, IMBA from Tsinghua (joint program with MIT), former IBM China strategy consultant; chairman since May 2021.

c1.evidence: KE leads China's housing-transaction platforms with RMB3,183.3 billion of 2025 GTV, but the industry is mature and shrinking rather than emerging, with GTV down 5.0% in 2025.

c2.evidence: Customers and agents choose Beike for its true-listing pledge, cross-brand Agent Cooperation Network and Lianjia service standards; the network is hard to copy, but brokerage services themselves are easy to substitute.

c3.evidence: Lianjia and Beike are household names in Chinese cities and the default leader in brokerage, but the brand is little known outside China and agents' service draws mixed reviews.

c4.evidence: Its mission 'admirable service, joyful living' is repeated in ESG and annual reports and the founders donated shares to an agents' health fund, but large founder share awards drew criticism in 2025-2026.

c6.evidence: “Lianjia agents, true listings, big platform, commissions” - the impression in China is mostly positive about reliability compared with other agencies, tempered by complaints about fees and agent pushiness.

c7.evidence: China's housing market is large but in secular decline; new commercial housing sales value fell 12.6% in 2025 to RMB8.39 trillion and demographics point to a smaller market.

c8.evidence: It has expanded into rentals (RMB21.9 billion revenue in 2025) and renovation (RMB15.4 billion), and is building AI tools for agents, but all expansion stays within Chinese housing.

m1.evidence: Peng has a clear vision of turning brokerage into a standardised, technology-driven service platform ('one body, three wings' of brokerage, renovation and rentals), but it is an evolutionary rather than world-changing vision.

m2.evidence: Peng co-founded the business, has led Lianjia/Beike since 2017 after joining Lianjia in 2010, and kept building through the 2021-2025 housing slump.

m4.evidence: Management emphasises agents' dignity and set up an employee health fund funded by founders' share donations, but agent headcount was cut (active agents down 7.5% year on year in Q2 2026).

m5.evidence: Lianjia's culture of standardised, honest listings and the ACN were deliberately built, and Beike launched VR viewing and AI tools, but invention is incremental.

m6.evidence: Peng has an electrical engineering degree and was a strategy consultant at IBM, and he champions the platform's technology, but he is more an operator and strategist than a product engineer.

m7.evidence: Peng and co-founder Shan donated shares to employee welfare funds, but large founder share-based compensation (over RMB3 billion combined in 2021-2024 per press reports) has drawn criticism.

m7b.evidence: We found no record of Peng giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Peng keeps a low public profile; he is not known for a distinctive public persona like the late founder Zuo Hui.

m9.evidence: Under Peng revenue rose from RMB70.5 billion in 2020 to RMB94.6 billion in 2025 and Q2 2026 net income doubled to RMB2.6 billion, but losses in 2021-2022 and falling GTV temper the record.

m10.evidence: Management cut operating expenses 14% year on year in Q2 2026 to RMB3.99 billion, but it is not known for a frugal culture and share-based pay has been large.

c10.evidence: Beike helps tens of millions of Chinese families find, buy and rent homes more safely, but its impact is limited to China.

p2.evidence: Building a trusted, cross-brand transaction network across about 60,000 stores is hard and matters to Chinese households, but brokerage is not technically hard to replicate locally.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew in four of the last five years (RMB70.5B in 2020 to RMB94.6B in 2025) but fell 24.9% in 2022, and H1 2026 revenue was down 12.0% year on year.

f2.evidence: Gross margin went from 23.9% in 2020 to 21.4% in 2025 and operating margin from 4.0% to 2.2%, though Q2 2026 margins rebounded to 28.6% and 12.3%.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 it had RMB47.0 billion of cash and short-term investments against about RMB1.7 billion of borrowings and related-party loans, with RMB65.6 billion of equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income fell from RMB2.84 billion in 2020 to RMB2.11 billion in 2025 and operating cash flow from RMB9.36 billion to an outflow of RMB0.38 billion.

v1.evidence: Beike's true-listing guarantee and huge shared inventory give buyers a practical reason to prefer it, but in many cities rival agencies and portals offer similar listings.

v2.evidence: We found no major employer ranking placing KE Holdings among the best places to work.

c5.evidence: Home buyers and renters in Chinese cities and about 540,000 agents on its platform would miss its listings, trust guarantees and transaction services, though other agencies would fill much of the gap.
